figures.caption: Figure 1: Pipeline of MEG data from preprocessing to the spatial effect estimation using model-based gradient boosting.

Figure 2: Examples of Wendland radial basis functions centered at different cortical locations. Left panel: Unscaled basis function evaluations; right panel: binary representation of regions covered by these particular basis functions.
Figure 3: Examples of simulated spatial Gaussian noise fields only for four distinct subjects (without signal or halo components).

Figure 4: Simulated signal plateau regions for both hemispheres. Colors indicate signal amplitudes τp, with positive (red) and negative (blue) activations represented by the color scales. Left panel: scenarios varying signs and varying amplitudes; right panel: scenarios varying signs and amplitudes and single signal.

Figure 5: Results for FPR (first row) and TPR (second row). The boosting approach is shown in red (Boosting) and cluster-based permutation tests in blue (CbPT). Columns correspond to the four simulation settings: varying signs, varying amplitudes, varying signs and amplitudes, and single signal.
Table 1: Estimation accuracy of the boosting approach across all simulation configurations.
Figure 6: Left panel: Observed centered differences of gamma-band activity between conditions, averaged across subjects; right panel: Results from cluster permutation tests on experimental data.
Figure 7: Empirical results from gradient boosted WRBF. Left panel: effect estimation; right panel: spatial regions covered by WRBF.
Figure 8: Examples of subject-level effects from the simulation setting varying signs and varying amplitudes.

Figure 9: Examples of simulated measurements averaged across N = 25 subjects. Each column represents another simulated experiment. First row: Scenarios varying signs and varying amplitudes; second row: scenario varying signs and amplitudes and single signal.

Figure 10: One example result from each simulation setting highlighting far more detailed results of the proposed boosting approach. Varying signs: high FPR for cluster-based permutation test (0.419) vs. only 0.157 for boosting). Varying amplitudes: high FPR for cluster-based permutation test (0.424) vs. only 0.162 for boosting). Varying signs and amplitudes: Rare example of boosting missing one signal (TPR: 0.67) and cluster-based permutation testing detects signal relatively well. Single signal: Identical results in terms of TPR (both 1) and FPR (both 0.132) .
Figure 11: Examples of subject-level centered difference measurements from real world experiment.

Figure 12: Simulation results for FPR (first row) and TPR (second row) of Bayes GLM. Columns correspond to the four simulation settings: varying signs, varying amplitudes, varying signs and amplitudes, and single signal. Thresholds are factors of the standard deviation: {0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8} · sd(measurement).

Figure 13: Simulation results for FPR (first row) and TPR (second row). The clusterbased permutation test is shown in red (CbPT), Bayes GLM in green (BayesGLM), and Boosting in blue (Boosting). Columns correspond to the four simulation settings: varying signs, varying amplitudes, varying signs and amplitudes, and single signal. Bayes GLM threshold: 0.2 · sd(measurement).
Table 2: MAE (top) and RMSE (bottom) for Bayes GLM, computed from the posterior mean field estimate, compared against the Wendland Boosting approach.
Figure 14: Empirical results from Bayes GLM with threshold 0.2 · sd(measurement), computed separately per hemisphere. Left panel: effect estimation; right panel: selected regions.
